heat_guidance.summary: Use the heat index (air temperature plus relative humidity, in shade) for the weather card, and WBGT when an on-site WBGT reading is available. Humid coastal cities can reach high heat index values even when the air temperature looks moderate.

heat_index_bands.effect: Below the lowest NWS heat index band.
heat_index_bands.suggested_action: Train and race as normal; drink to thirst.

heat_index_bands.effect: Fatigue possible with prolonged exposure and/or physical activity.
heat_index_bands.suggested_action: Start early, carry fluids on long sessions, and expect slower paces.

heat_index_bands.effect: Heat stroke, heat cramps, or heat exhaustion possible with prolonged exposure and/or physical activity.
heat_index_bands.suggested_action: Shorten or ease hard efforts, take extra breaks in shade, and use aid stations; unacclimatised athletes should hold back.

heat_index_bands.effect: Heat cramps or heat exhaustion likely, and heat stroke possible with prolonged exposure and/or physical activity.
heat_index_bands.suggested_action: Avoid hard or long outdoor efforts; organisers should consider delaying, shortening or rescheduling.

heat_index_notes: Effects are NWS wording; suggested actions are StartLine guidance built on those effects and on NATA's advice to delay, reschedule or shorten sessions in stressful heat.
NWS heat index values assume shade; full sun can raise the heat index by up to 15 F (about 8 C).
Celsius ranges are converted from the NWS Fahrenheit bands.

To compute the heat index from temperature and relative humidity, use the NWS Rothfusz regression with its low and high humidity adjustments; the regression applies when the simple formula gives 80 F (26.7 C) or more.

wbgt_bands.guidance: Normal activities; at least 3 rest breaks per hour of at least 3 minutes each.
Use discretion for intense or prolonged exercise and watch at-risk athletes; at least 3 rest breaks per hour of at least 4 minutes each.
Limit sessions to 2 hours; at least 4 rest breaks per hour of at least 4 minutes each.
Limit sessions to 1 hour with 20 minutes of rest breaks within the hour.
No outdoor workouts; delay until a cooler WBGT reading.

wbgt_notes: WBGT combines temperature, humidity, sun and wind, so it reflects heat stress better than air temperature alone.

These bands are the example table in the NATA 2015 position statement, taken from Georgia (USA) high school guidelines; NATA says WBGT thresholds should be adjusted to the local climate, so treat them as a guide.
practical_points: Acclimatise gradually over 7 to 14 days before racing in heat; the benefit fades within about 3 weeks without heat exposure (NATA Recommendation 2).
Drink enough to avoid losing more than 2% of body mass during a session (NATA Recommendation 4).

Treat any collapse in the heat as possible exertional heat stroke: cold-water immersion is the most effective cooling, and patients should be cooled first and transported second when medical staff are on site (NATA Recommendations 38 and 41).
When conditions are stressful, delay, reschedule or shorten the session (NATA Recommendation 10).

air_quality_guidance.text: CPCB's National AQI has six categories: Good (0-50), Satisfactory (51-100), Moderate (101-200), Poor (201-300), Very Poor (301-400) and Severe (401-500). The city figure in CPCB's daily bulletin is the 24-hour average up to 4 PM, set by the worst pollutant and averaged across the city's stations.

CPCB health statements: Satisfactory can cause minor breathing discomfort to sensitive people; Moderate, breathing discomfort for people with lung disease, asthma or heart disease; Poor, breathing discomfort for most people on prolonged exposure; Very Poor, respiratory illness on prolonged exposure; Severe affects healthy people too.

When to reduce intensity: at Moderate, athletes with asthma or heart conditions should shorten and ease hard sessions and keep reliever medicine handy; at Poor, everyone should cut long or intense outdoor efforts and take more breaks; at Very Poor or Severe, move training indoors or reschedule. This applies CPCB's health statements using US EPA activity advice, which is written for the US AQI scale, so it is guidance rather than an official CPCB rule.

On polluted days, choose a less intense activity, shorten the session or reschedule it, and exercise away from busy roads. Check the station nearest the venue on race morning, because CPCB's city figure averages all stations and individual locations can differ.
